characters: Ama: a girl of about five, braided hair with yellow ribbons, a blue dress, bare feet or simple sandals.
Pepe: a small brown goat with one white spot on his nose.
Grandpa Yaw: a kind elderly man with a white beard and a walking stick.
The hen: a speckled hen with four chicks.

narrationPlan.voice: Warm female storyteller, Ghanaian English (en-GH), unhurried.
narrationPlan.pace: Slow (about 100 words per minute) for the youngest listeners.
notes: Distinct but gentle voices for the hen and Grandpa Yaw.
Leave about 0.6 s of silence between pages.
Goat bleats performed by the narrator, not sound-effect files, so timing stays exact.

ama-lost-little-goat.music: Optional soft village morning ambience (kalimba and light percussion). Not created; needs a verified licence before use.
culturalNotes: Ama and Yaw are Akan day names (born on Saturday / Thursday). A Ghanaian reviewer should confirm they are used naturally.
Free-roaming goats tied with rope near a family compound are common in villages.
reviewQuestions: Is "Grandpa Yaw" a natural form of address for this setting?
Is the level right for Nursery 2 to KG 1 listeners (sentence length, vocabulary)?

pages.brief: Warm morning light. Ama hugging Pepe in front of a family compound. The white spot on Pepe’s nose clearly visible.
pages.narration: Warm and gentle. Slight smile on "Pepe". Pause after "village".

pages.brief: Ama kneeling with a bowl of water and leaves, Pepe eating. Sunlit yard, hens in the background.
pages.narration: Playful. Perform "Meh-eh-eh!" as a goat bleat, short and funny.

pages.brief: Empty rope on the post, Ama with bucket and worried face. Keep it gentle, not scary.
pages.narration: Surprise on "gone!", then worried calling. Slow down on "Pepe! Pepe!".

pages.brief: Big mango tree, hen with four chicks, Ama crouching to ask. Speech is implied by posture only.
pages.narration: Hen voice is clucky and kind. Pause before "Try near the well".

pages.brief: Village well with stone rim, Grandpa Yaw leaning on his stick, pointing gently toward a big rock in the distance.
pages.narration: Grandpa Yaw: slow, warm, a little slower than the narrator.

pages.brief: Large grey rock, Pepe tangled gently in a rope on a low branch, Ama running toward him with joy and relief.
pages.narration: Build excitement. Short silence after "listened", then the bleat, then joy on "It was Pepe!".

pages.brief: Ama untangling the rope, Pepe nuzzling, Grandpa Yaw and the hen watching warmly from the edge.
pages.narration: Tender and relieved. Smile on "licked her hand".

pages.brief: Golden sunset, Pepe curled up asleep by a strong post, Ama whispering to him.
pages.narration: Slow, soft, sleepy. Whisper "Stay close, little one". Long pause before "The end".

characters: Kofi: a boy of about six in a green T-shirt and shorts, round glasses optional, always smiling.
Maame (Kofi’s mother): a kind woman in a patterned wrapper cloth and headscarf.

narrationPlan.voice: Friendly storyteller, Ghanaian English, bright and encouraging.
narrationPlan.pace: Slow to medium; slower still on counting passages.
notes: Leave a beat after each number on pages 5 and 6 so children can count aloud.
Sing or hum the garden song briefly on page 4 (not a copyrighted tune).

kofis-colourful-garden.music: Optional light, cheerful ambience (birdsong and soft marimba). Not created; needs a verified licence.
culturalNotes: Maame means "mother" in Akan. Okra, corn, tomatoes and carrots are common household garden crops.
reviewQuestions: Are carrots a realistic crop for the intended audience, or should garden eggs or peppers replace them?

pages.brief: Behind-the-house yard, bare soil patch, Kofi receiving small seed packets from Maame. Morning light.
pages.narration: Bright and curious. Slight lift on "garden".

pages.brief: Close view of Kofi’s hands placing a seed, watering can, neat row of little holes.
pages.narration: Slow and careful, matching the actions.

pages.brief: Three small sun or moon marks in the sky to show days passing, Kofi peering at empty soil.
pages.narration: Count the days slowly. Soft puzzled tone on "sleeping".

pages.brief: Kofi singing with watering can, one tiny green sprout glowing slightly in the foreground.
pages.narration: Hum a few notes for the song. Gasp of delight before "something small and green".

pages.brief: Garden bed with three clearly separate red tomatoes and two green okra pods, easy to count.
pages.narration: Pause after each number so a child can count along.

pages.brief: Four corn cobs and five carrot tops, clearly separated for counting. Kofi pointing as he counts.
pages.narration: Slow counting, one beat per number.

pages.brief: Kofi holding up a full basket, Maame smiling, rainbow of vegetables in the basket.
pages.narration: Proud and joyful. Name each colour clearly.

pages.brief: Cosy evening kitchen, steaming pot, Kofi and Maame at the table.
pages.narration: Warm, satisfied. Gentle pause before "The end".

characters: Tortoise (Ɔkoto-style storyteller tortoise): old, slow, bright-eyed, with a patterned shell.
Hare: quick, quick to laugh, long ears.
Heron: tall, grey-white, calm.
Ants: a line of small ants carrying white eggs.

narrationPlan.voice: Experienced storyteller, Ghanaian English, with distinct (not cartoonish) voices for Tortoise, Hare and Heron.
narrationPlan.pace: Medium (about 120 words per minute); slower for Tortoise.
notes: Folktale cadence with light call-and-response feel.
Storm passage can build in volume but must stay comfortable at classroom speaker levels.
Verify pronunciation of "swallows" and "riverbank" with the narrator.

clever-tortoise-and-the-rain.music: Optional gentle drums and shaker underscore for the dig and the storm (ducked under narration). Not created; needs a verified licence.
culturalNotes: Trickster and wise-animal tales are widespread in Ghanaian oral tradition. This is an original retelling that borrows the tradition’s spirit, not a copy of any specific recorded tale.
A cultural reviewer should check that the portrayal of elders and community work feels authentic.
reviewQuestions: Is the ending proverb natural? Consider whether a known Akan proverb would fit better.
Reading level: some sentences are long for Primary 2; consider simplifying pages 2 and 8.

pages.brief: Wide dry landscape, nearly dry river, yellow grass, heat haze. Animals small in the distance, drooping.
pages.narration: Slow and heavy. Let the heat be felt in the pace.

pages.brief: Close portrait of Tortoise on the bank, wise eyes. Include small details: ants, birds, clouds far away.
pages.narration: Tortoise’s saying slowly and warmly, like a grandparent.

pages.brief: Macro view of ants carrying eggs up a slope, Tortoise’s curious face in the corner.
pages.narration: Curious, wondering tone on the question.

pages.brief: Swallows low over the grass, a darker line of cloud on the horizon, Tortoise sniffing the air.
pages.narration: Quiet certainty. Slow down on "I am sure of it".

pages.brief: Hare in comic laughter, Heron attentive, Tortoise calm. Keep the laughter friendly, not cruel.
pages.narration: Hare’s voice quick and teasing. Heron’s voice calm and low.

pages.brief: Tortoise drawing a circle in the dirt with a claw, Heron nodding, a hillside behind them.
pages.narration: Thoughtful, explaining. Heron’s “I will help” is simple and firm.

pages.brief: A busy dig site with animals of every size working together, Hare joining at the edge.
pages.narration: Rhythm of work. Gentle humour on Hare’s sigh.

pages.brief: Dramatic but safe night rain, lightning far away, water streaming into the dug hole. Comforting, not frightening.
pages.narration: Build with the storm, then calm to wonder on the last sentence.

pages.brief: Pond full of clear water, Hare bowing his head to Tortoise, other animals drinking in the background.
pages.narration: Sincere and a little shy for Hare.

pages.brief: Golden-hour scene, animals resting around the pond, Tortoise and Hare side by side.
pages.narration: Warm and wise. Slow the final line. Pause before "The end".

characters: Amina: a girl of six with a bright smile, school uniform (blue and white), small red backpack.
Madam Abena: a friendly young teacher with a warm smile and a lanyard.
Salifu: a boy of six, cheerful, a little taller than Amina, same uniform.
Mama: Amina’s mother, in a bright headscarf.

narrationPlan.voice: Warm, reassuring storyteller, Ghanaian English. Different gentle voices for Mama, Madam Abena and Salifu.
narrationPlan.pace: Slow to medium (about 110 words per minute).
notes: The bell is performed vocally ("ding-dong") on page 3.
Amina’s whisper must stay audible on classroom speakers.

aminas-first-day-at-school.music: Optional light school-morning ambience (distant children, soft guitar). Not created; needs a verified licence.
culturalNotes: Amina and Salifu are common Muslim names in northern Ghana; Madam Abena is an Akan day name. Names are chosen to reflect Ghana’s diversity and need reviewer confirmation.
Uniform colours are illustrative; a reviewer should confirm they feel typical.
reviewQuestions: Should the school setting be made more specific (town or region) or kept general?
Is the word "nervous" appropriate for KG 2 or should it be "worried"?

pages.brief: Amina at home in her uniform, hand on her tummy, a few playful butterfly shapes around her tummy area (a drawing device, not real insects).
pages.narration: Gentle and relatable. Smile on "butterflies were dancing".

pages.brief: Mother and daughter walking, school gate in the distance, morning sun.
pages.narration: Mama’s voice is calm and reassuring.

pages.brief: Busy school gate, blurred running children, Amina still and small in the centre.
pages.narration: Perform the bell. Slow and small on the whisper.

pages.brief: Madam Abena kneeling, eye to eye with Amina, warm expression.
pages.narration: Madam Abena: bright and kind, never rushed.

pages.brief: Shared desk, Salifu offering three crayons, Amina listening shyly.
pages.narration: Salifu cheerful and friendly. Name the colours clearly.

pages.brief: Close view of a shared drawing: big yellow sun and green tree, both children smiling.
pages.narration: Calm, easing. Slow on "quiet".

pages.brief: Playground circle, children clapping in pairs, Amina laughing with Salifu.
pages.narration: Lively, with a bouncy clapping rhythm.

pages.brief: Afternoon light, Amina running to Mama waving her drawing.
pages.narration: Joyful. Pause before "The end".

characters: Little Star: a very small, round, glowing star with a gentle smiling face.
Big Star and Moon: large, kind and calm.
Traveller: a woman carrying a bundle on her head, walking home along a path at night.

narrationPlan.voice: Soft, soothing lullaby-style storyteller (en-GH or en-GB). Slightly deeper voice for the Moon.
narrationPlan.pace: Very slow (about 90 words per minute); designed to be a bedtime read.
notes: The "Shine, shine, shine" chant is a repeated refrain: keep the rhythm identical each time.
Final page should fade into a whisper.

little-star-that-loved-to-shine.music: Optional gentle music-box lullaby (original composition or properly licensed). Ducks under narration. Not created.
culturalNotes: The story is universal and sets no specific culture. A Ghanaian version (traveller, setting, names) could be offered later as a localised variant.
reviewQuestions: Should the traveller and path be made explicitly Ghanaian (a village path)?
Is "peeping" a known word for this age or should it be "shining"?

pages.brief: Deep indigo sky, many stars, one small golden star with a face in the centre.
pages.narration: Slow, hushed, lullaby-like. Elongate "very, very small".

pages.brief: Little star glowing next to huge bright stars that look almost like suns.
pages.narration: A gentle chant on "shine, shine, shine".

pages.brief: Little star with downcast expression, softer glow.
pages.narration: Soft and sad, but not heavy.

pages.brief: Gentle crescent moon with a kind face, little star looking up to it.
pages.narration: Moon: deep, slow and comforting.

pages.brief: Dark path through gentle hills, a woman with a bundle on her head walking, cloud covering most stars.
pages.narration: Quiet, a little tense but safe. Slow, whispering.

pages.brief: A single gap in the clouds with the little star shining, the traveller looking up in hope.
pages.narration: Pause before "Then she saw". Wonder.

pages.brief: A soft pool of starlight on the path, footsteps leading along it.
pages.narration: Count steps slowly. The "shine" chant returns, more confident.

pages.brief: Warm lit doorway, the traveller waving at the sky, little star glowing happily.
pages.narration: Whisper. Slow right down, like falling asleep. Long pause before "The end".

characters: Efua: a girl of thirteen, JHS uniform, practical and thoughtful.
Kwabena: her classmate, confident and always looking for shortcuts.
Auntie Dede: a market trader who gives Efua advice.

narrationPlan.voice: Natural, mature storyteller, Ghanaian English. Subtle character differences, no caricature.
notes: Numbers must be spoken clearly and consistently with the text (check twelve, eight, forty, twenty, twenty-five).

efuas-honest-business.music: No background music: text-first reading experience for older learners. Optional soft ambience toggle only.
culturalNotes: Groundnut cakes (and similar snacks) are a familiar local treat; a reviewer should confirm the recipe description and the realism of prices in cedis for the intended year.
reviewQuestions: Are the prices realistic for the intended region and year? (Amounts are illustrative.)
Does the dilemma suit JHS and avoid moralising?

pages.brief: Kitchen scene, grandmother teaching Efua to shape cakes, cooking pot, warm light.
pages.narration: Calm, thoughtful teen narrator.

pages.brief: Close view of the exercise book with simple costing sums (legible but illustrative), Efua concentrating.
pages.narration: Measured, working-it-out pace. Slow on the numbers.

pages.brief: School gate at close of day, Efua with a tray of packs, students queuing, Kwabena watching from the side.
pages.narration: Pace picks up for sales, then slows with tension on "pulled her aside".

pages.brief: Kwabena leaning in conspiratorially, Efua’s uncertain expression. Not villainous, just persuasive.
pages.narration: Kwabena: smooth, confident, reasonable-sounding.

pages.brief: Evening room, single lamp, Efua with her book, thoughtful, moon outside the window.
pages.narration: Slow, reflective. Let the sums breathe.

pages.brief: Busy market stall, Auntie Dede with baskets, kindly expression, Efua listening.
pages.narration: Auntie Dede: warm, firm, experienced.

pages.brief: Close-up of Efua’s hands filling a pack and labelling the date, growing queue in the background.
pages.narration: Quiet pride. Steady pace.

pages.brief: Longer queue at the school gate, Kwabena in the line, Efua smiling and handing him a pack.
pages.narration: Satisfied, understated. A smile in the voice on the last line.
